description.summary: Mogwai (魔鬼, Cantonese mō gwái) is a Chinese term for demons, devils, or evil spirits, denoting a category of malevolent supernatural beings in Chinese folk and religious traditions.
description.full: Mogwai is the Cantonese romanisation of the Chinese 魔鬼 (Mandarin mógui), a term used in Chinese folk religion, popular Buddhism, and Daoism for demons, devils, or malevolent spirits. The first character 魔 (mó) derives ultimately from the Sanskrit māra (मार), originally meaning 'death' or 'evil being', a term that entered Chinese with the spread of Buddhism. The second character 鬼 (gui) refers to ghosts or spirits, particularly the souls of departed beings. In Chinese tradition mogwai (mógui) are commonly distinguished from neighbouring categories: yāoguài (妖怪, goblins or sprites associated with abnormal phenomena), guǐ (鬼, ghosts), and guài (怪, strange phenomena). Mogwai broadly denotes demonic adversaries, including beings adopted from Indian Buddhism such as yakshas (yecha 夜叉) and rakshasas (luocha 罗刹), which appear extensively in classical literature including Pu Songling's Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio (Liaozhai zhiyi) and the Ming-dynasty novel Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi). The English-language word 'mogwai' was popularised in the Western world by the 1984 Joe Dante film Gremlins, which used the term for its furry creatures; that usage is a borrowing of the Chinese name and not the traditional Chinese referent.

etymology.origin: Cantonese romanisation of Chinese 魔鬼; the character 魔 (mó) derives from Sanskrit māra ('death' / 'evil being'), entering Chinese through Buddhist scripture translation.
etymology.first_use: The compound 魔鬼 has been used in Chinese-Buddhist contexts since at least the medieval period; the romanisation 'mogwai' is a 20th-century Cantonese-English convention popularised in the West by Gremlins (1984).

related_phenomena.name: Yaoguai
related_phenomena.description: Chinese category of goblins / sprites (妖怪)

related_phenomena.name: Rakshasa
related_phenomena.description: Indian-origin man-eating demon (luocha 罗刹) absorbed into Chinese demonology

features.description: Mogwai have no single fixed appearance; classical sources describe them taking many shapes appropriate to their type
Air-traversing yecha (yakshas) are described as winged with red, blue, or yellow complexions
Earth-traversing yecha are described as several metres tall with distinctive markings

physical.morphology: No single fixed morphology; mogwai is a category that includes a range of demonic forms drawn from indigenous Chinese tradition and from Buddhist sources of Indian origin.

abilities.description: Believed to afflict humans with misfortune, illness, or moral corruption
In classical tales (e.g. Liaozhai zhiyi) demonic beings often take human form to deceive mortals
Some folk traditions hold that rain-demons mate during seasonal rainfall, taken as a sign of prosperity

patterns: Tempt and afflict humans, particularly the morally weak
Appear in literary tales as antagonists testing virtue
Inhabit boundaries between human and wild / between living and dead worlds

range.description: Mogwai are part of the broad Chinese demonological tradition and appear throughout Chinese-speaking cultures and the Sinosphere (where Chinese Buddhism and Daoism shaped local folklore).
regions: Sinosphere (Vietnam, Korea, Japan via Buddhist transmission)

peak_activity_periods.description: Major literary period for tales of demons and supernatural encounters, including Pu Songling's Liaozhai zhiyi and Investiture of the Gods

origins.cultural_roots: Chinese folk religion, Daoism, and Chinese Buddhism. The character 魔 (mó) was adopted to render the Sanskrit māra in Buddhist translation.
origins.earliest_accounts: Mogwai-class beings (especially yecha and luocha) appear in Chinese-language Buddhist scripture and in literary tales from the medieval period onward.
origins.folklore_connections: Connected to Indian Buddhist demonology (yakshas, rakshasas) and to indigenous Chinese categories of spirits (gui, yaoguai, guai).

timeline.event: Sanskrit māra rendered as Chinese 魔; absorbed into Chinese-language Buddhist scripture and demonology
timeline.significance: Establishes the term and concept of mogui in Chinese

timeline.event: Yecha and luocha appear prominently in Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi)
timeline.significance: Demons enter major Chinese popular literature

timeline.event: Pu Songling's Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio (Liaozhai zhiyi) collects many tales of demonic encounters
Joe Dante's film Gremlins introduces 'mogwai' as a name for furry creatures, popularising the Chinese word in the English-speaking world
timeline.significance: Western popular-culture borrowing of the term

history.modern_era: In contemporary Chinese-language usage 魔鬼 (mogui / mogwai) remains a common word for 'demon' or 'devil' in religious, literary, and metaphorical contexts. In English the word is most strongly associated with the 1984 film Gremlins and its derivatives, which is a Western re-borrowing rather than a faithful representation of Chinese folklore.

paranormal.name: Traditional Chinese demonology
paranormal.description: In Chinese folk religion, Daoism and Buddhism, mogwai are real malevolent spiritual beings to be guarded against through ritual, virtuous conduct and protective practice.

skeptical.name: Cultural and literary construct
skeptical.description: From a secular perspective mogwai are figures of religion and literature rather than empirical entities; the category functions as a shared symbolic vocabulary for danger, moral failure, and the wild.
evidence_cited: Documented evolution of the term within textual tradition

stories: Tales from Pu Songling's Liaozhai zhiyi (Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio)
Episodes from Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi)
folklore.beliefs: Mogwai represent real malevolent forces in Chinese folk and religious thought, to be countered by virtuous conduct, Buddhist or Daoist ritual, and protective talismans.

literature: Liaozhai zhiyi (Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio) — Pu Songling (Qing dynasty)
Fengshen Yanyi (Investiture of the Gods) — Ming dynasty
film_tv: Gremlins: Secrets of the Mogwai (2023, animated)
music: Mogwai (Scottish post-rock band, named after the term)

research.ongoing_studies: Mogwai are studied as part of academic Chinese religion, folklore and literature scholarship rather than cryptozoology.
